In mathematics, a [[Derivation (differential algebra)|derivation]] <math>\partial</math> of a [[commutative ring]] <math>A</math> is called a '''locally nilpotent derivation''' ('''LND''') if every element of <math>A</math> is annihilated by some power of <math>\partial</math>. 
<!-- In [[algebra]], a locally nilpotent derivation of a [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]] is a special kind of a [[Derivation (differential algebra)|derivation]] of a ring.-->

One motivation for the study of locally nilpotent derivations comes from the fact that some of the counterexamples to [[Hilbert's 14th problem]] are obtained as the kernels of a derivation on a [[polynomial ring]].<ref>{{cite web |last=Daigle |first=Daniel |title=Hilbert's Fourteenth Problem and Locally Nilpotent Derivations |url=http://aix1.uottawa.ca/~ddaigle/articles/H14survey.pdf |website=[[University of Ottawa]] |access-date=11 September 2018}}</ref>

Over a field <math>k</math> of characteristic zero, to give a locally nilpotent derivation on the integral domain <math>A</math>, finitely generated over the field, is equivalent to giving an action of the [[additive group]] <math>(k,+)</math> to the affine variety <math>X = \operatorname{Spec}(A)</math>. Roughly speaking, an affine variety admitting "plenty" of actions of the additive group is considered similar to an [[affine space]].<ref name="AFKKZ">{{cite journal| last1=Arzhantsev|first1=I.|last2=Flenner|first2=H.|last3=Kaliman|first3=S.|last4=Kutzschebauch|first4=F.| last5=Zaidenberg|first5=M.|title=Flexible varieties and automorphism groups|journal=Duke Math. J.|date=2013|volume=162| issue=4|pages=767–823|doi=10.1215/00127094-2080132|arxiv=1011.5375|s2cid=53412676 }}</ref><!-- In affine [[algebraic geometry]], locally nilpotent derivations are used to study derivations are used to study <math>(\mathbb{C},+)</math>-actions on affine varieties. Roughly speaking, an affine variety <math>X</math> over <math>\mathbb{C}</math> is considered to be [[Flexible variety|flexible]], and thus similar to an affine space, if <math>X</math> admits plenty of such actions, or equivalently, if its coordinate ring <math>\mathbb{C}[X]</math> has a lot of locally nilpotent derivations.-->

== Definition ==
Let <math>A</math> be a [[Ring (mathematics)|ring]]. Recall that a [[Derivation (differential algebra)|derivation]] of <math>A</math> is a map <math>\partial\colon\, A\to A </math> satisfying the [[product rule|Leibniz rule]] <math>\partial (ab)=(\partial a)b+a(\partial b)</math> for any <math>a,b\in A </math>.  If <math>A</math> is an [[Algebra over a field|algebra]] over a field <math>k</math>, we additionally require <math>\partial</math> to be <math>k</math>-linear, so <math>k\subseteq \ker \partial</math>.

A derivation <math>\partial</math> is called a ''locally nilpotent derivation'' (LND) if for every <math>a \in A</math>, there exists a positive integer  <math>n</math> such that <math>\partial^{n}(a)=0</math>.

If <math>A</math> is [[Graded ring|graded]], we say that a locally nilpotent derivation <math>\partial</math> is ''homogeneous'' (of degree <math>d</math>) if <math>\deg \partial a=\deg a +d</math> for every <math>a\in A</math>.

The set of locally nilpotent derivations of a ring <math>A</math> is denoted by <math>\operatorname{LND}(A)</math>. Note that this set has no obvious structure: it is neither closed under addition (e.g. if  <math>\partial_{1}=y\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x}</math>, <math>\partial_{2}=x\tfrac{\partial}{\partial y}</math> then <math>\partial_{1},\partial_{2}\in \operatorname{LND}(k[x,y])</math> but <math>(\partial_{1}+\partial_{2})^{2}(x)=x</math>, so <math>\partial_{1}+\partial_{2}\not\in \operatorname{LND}(k[x,y])</math>) nor under multiplication by elements of <math>A</math> (e.g. <math>\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\in \operatorname{LND}(k[x])</math>, but <math>x\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\not\in\operatorname{LND}(k[x])</math>). However, if <math>[\partial_{1},\partial_{2}]=0</math> then <math>\partial_{1},\partial_{2}\in \operatorname{LND}(A)</math> implies <math>\partial_{1}+\partial_{2}\in \operatorname{LND}(A)</math><ref name="Freudenburg" /> and if <math>\partial\in \operatorname{LND}(A)</math>, <math>h\in\ker\partial</math> then <math>h\partial\in \operatorname{LND}(A)</math>.

== Relation to {{math|'''G'''<sub>''a''</sub>}}-actions ==
Let <math>A</math> be an algebra over a field <math>k</math> of characteristic zero (e.g. <math>k=\mathbb{C}</math>). Then there is a one-to-one correspondence between the locally nilpotent <math>k</math>-derivations on <math>A</math> and the [[Group-scheme action|actions]] of the additive group <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math> of <math>k</math> on the affine variety <math>\operatorname{Spec} A</math>, as follows.<ref name="Freudenburg">{{cite book|last1=Freudenburg|first1=G.|title=Algebraic theory of locally nilpotent derivations|date=2006|publisher=Springer-Verlag|location=Berlin| isbn=978-3-540-29521-1| citeseerx=10.1.1.470.10}}</ref> 
A <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math>-action on <math>\operatorname{Spec} A</math> corresponds to a <math>k</math>-algebra homomorphism <math>\rho\colon A\to A[t]</math>. Any such <math>\rho</math> determines a locally nilpotent derivation <math>\partial</math> of <math>A</math> by taking its derivative at zero, namely <math>\partial=\epsilon \circ \tfrac{d}{dt}\circ \rho,</math> where <math>\epsilon</math> denotes the evaluation at <math>t=0</math>. 
Conversely, any locally nilpotent derivation <math>\partial</math> determines a homomorphism <math>\rho\colon A\to A[t]</math> by <math> \rho = \exp (t\partial)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^{n}}{n!}\partial^{n}.</math>

It is easy to see that the conjugate actions correspond to conjugate derivations, i.e. if <math>\alpha\in \operatorname{Aut} A</math> and <math>\partial\in \operatorname{LND}(A)</math> then <math>\alpha\circ\partial \circ \alpha^{-1}\in \operatorname{LND}(A)</math> and <math>\exp(t\cdot \alpha\circ\partial \circ \alpha^{-1})=\alpha \circ \exp(t\partial)\circ \alpha^{-1}</math>

== The kernel algorithm ==
The algebra <math>\ker \partial</math> consists of the invariants of the corresponding <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math>-action. It is algebraically and factorially closed in <math>A</math>.<ref name="Freudenburg" /> A special case of [[Hilbert's fourteenth problem|Hilbert's 14th problem]] asks whether <math>\ker \partial</math> is finitely generated, or, if <math>A=k[X]</math>, whether the [[GIT quotient|quotient]] <math>X/\!/\mathbb{G}_{a}</math> is affine. By [[Zariski's finiteness theorem]],<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Zariski|first1=O.|title=Interprétations algébrico-géométriques du quatorzième problème de Hilbert|journal=Bull. Sci. Math. (2)|date=1954|volume=78|pages=155–168}}</ref> it is true if <math>\dim X\leq 3</math>. On the other hand, this question is highly nontrivial even for <math>X=\mathbb{C}^{n}</math>, <math>n\geq 4</math>. For <math>n\geq 5</math> the answer, in general, is negative.<ref name="derksen">{{cite journal|last1=Derksen|first1=H. G. J.|title=The kernel of a derivation|journal=J. Pure Appl. Algebra|date=1993|volume=84|issue=1|pages=13–16|doi=10.1016/0022-4049(93)90159-Q|doi-access=free}}</ref> The case <math>n=4</math> is open.<ref name="Freudenburg" />

However, in practice it often happens that <math>\ker\partial</math> is known to be finitely generated: notably, by the Maurer&ndash;Weitzenböck theorem,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Seshadri|first1=C.S.|title=On a theorem of Weitzenböck in invariant theory|journal=J. Math. Kyoto Univ.|date=1962|volume=1|issue=3|pages=403–409|doi=10.1215/kjm/1250525012|url=https://projecteuclid.org/download/pdf_1/euclid.kjm/1250525012|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription}}</ref> it is the case for ''linear'' LND's of the polynomial algebra over a field of characteristic zero (by ''linear'' we mean homogeneous of degree zero with respect to the standard grading).

Assume <math>\ker \partial</math> is finitely generated. If <math>A=k[g_1,\dots, g_n]</math> is a [[finitely generated algebra]] over a field of characteristic zero, then <math>\ker\partial</math> can be computed using van den Essen's algorithm,<ref name="van den Essen">{{cite book|last1=van den Essen|first1=A.|title=Polynomial automorphisms and the Jacobian conjecture|date=2000|publisher=Birkhäuser Verlag|location=Basel|isbn=978-3-7643-6350-5|doi=10.1007/978-3-0348-8440-2|s2cid=252433637 }}</ref> as follows. Choose a ''local slice'', i.e. an element <math>r\in \ker \partial^{2}\setminus \ker \partial</math> and put <math>f=\partial r\in \ker\partial</math>. Let <math>\pi_{r}\colon\, A\to (\ker \partial)_{f}</math> be the ''Dixmier map'' given by <math>\pi_{r}(a)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}}{n!}\partial^{n}(a)\frac{r^{n}}{f^{n}}</math>. Now for every <math>i=1,\dots, n</math>, chose a minimal integer <math>m_{i}</math> such that <math>h_{i}\colon = f^{m_{i}}\pi_{r}(g_{i})\in \ker\partial</math>, put <math>B_{0}=k[h_{1},\dots, h_{n},f]\subseteq \ker \partial</math>, and define inductively <math>B_{i}</math> to be the subring of <math>A</math> generated by <math> \{h\in A: fh\in B_{i-1}\}</math>. By induction, one proves that <math>B_{0}\subset B_{1}\subset \dots \subset\ker \partial </math> are finitely generated and if <math>B_{i}=B_{i+1}</math> then <math>B_{i}=\ker \partial</math>, so <math>B_{N}=\ker \partial</math> for some <math>N</math>. Finding the generators of each <math>B_{i}</math> and checking whether <math>B_{i}=B_{i+1}</math> is a standard computation using [[Gröbner bases]].<ref name="van den Essen" />

== Slice theorem ==
Assume that <math>\partial\in\operatorname{LND}(A)</math> admits a ''slice'', i.e. <math>s\in A</math> such that <math>\partial s=1</math>. The ''slice theorem''<ref name="Freudenburg" /> asserts that <math>A</math> is a polynomial algebra <math>(\ker\partial) [s]</math> and <math>\partial=\tfrac{d}{ds}</math>.

For any local slice <math>r\in\ker\partial \setminus \ker\partial^{2}</math> we can apply the slice theorem to the [[Localization of a ring|localization]] <math>A_{\partial r}</math>, and thus obtain that <math>A</math> is ''locally'' a polynomial algebra with a standard derivation. In geometric terms, if a [[geometric quotient]] <math>\pi\colon\,X\to X//\mathbb{G}_{a}</math> is affine (e.g. when <math>\dim X\leq 3</math> by the [[Zariski's finiteness theorem|Zariski theorem]]), then it has a Zariski-open subset <math>U</math> such that <math>\pi^{-1}(U)</math> is isomorphic over <math>U</math> to <math>U\times \mathbb{A}^{1}</math>, where <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math> acts by translation on the second factor.

However, in general it is not true that <math>X\to X//\mathbb{G}_{a}</math> is locally trivial. For example,<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Deveney|first1=J.|last2=Finston|first2=D.|title=A proper <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math>-action on <math>\mathbb{C}^{5}</math> which is not locally trivial|journal=[[Proc. Amer. Math. Soc.]]|date=1995|volume=123|issue=3|pages=651–655| doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1995-1273487-0 |doi-access=free|jstor=2160782}}</ref> let <math>\partial=u\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x}+v\tfrac{\partial}{\partial y}+(1+uy^2)\tfrac{\partial}{\partial z}\in \operatorname{LND}(\mathbb{C}[x,y,z,u,v])</math>. Then <math>\ker\partial</math> is a coordinate ring of a singular variety, and the fibers of the quotient map over singular points are two-dimensional.

If <math>\dim X=3</math> then <math>\Gamma=X\setminus U</math> is a curve. To describe the <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math>-action, it is important to understand the geometry <math>\Gamma</math>. Assume further that <math>k=\mathbb{C}</math> and that <math>X</math> is [[Smooth variety|smooth]] and [[contractible]] (in which case <math>S</math> is smooth and contractible as well<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kaliman|first1=S|last2=Saveliev|first2=N.|title=<math>\mathbb{C}_{+}</math>-Actions on contractible threefolds|journal=Michigan Math. J.|date=2004|volume=52|issue=3|pages=619–625|doi=10.1307/mmj/1100623416|url=https://projecteuclid.org/download/pdf_1/euclid.mmj/1100623416|arxiv=math/0209306|s2cid=15020160}}</ref>) and choose <math>\Gamma</math> to be minimal (with respect to inclusion). Then [[Shulim Kaliman|Kaliman]] proved<ref name="Kaliman" /> that each irreducible component of <math>\Gamma</math> is a ''polynomial curve'', i.e. its [[Normalization of an algebraic variety|normalization]] is isomorphic to <math>\mathbb{C}^{1}</math>. The curve <math>\Gamma</math> for the action given by Freudenburg's (2,5)-derivation (see [[#Examples|below]]) is a union of two lines in <math>\mathbb{C}^{2}</math>, so <math>\Gamma</math> may not be irreducible. However, it is conjectured that <math>\Gamma</math> is always [[contractible]].<ref name="Seattle">{{cite book| last1=Kaliman|first1=S.| contribution=Actions of <math>\mathbb{C}^{*}</math> and <math>\mathbb{C}_{+}</math> on affine algebraic varieties| date=2009|title=Algebraic geometry-Seattle 2005. Part 2|volume=80| pages=629–654|doi=10.1090/pspum/080.2/2483949|contribution-url=http://www.math.miami.edu/~kaliman/library/seattle.paper.pdf|series=Proceedings of Symposia in Pure Mathematics|isbn=9780821847039}}</ref>

== Examples ==
=== Example 1 ===
The standard coordinate derivations <math>\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x_i}</math> of a polynomial algebra <math>k[x_1,\dots, x_n]</math> are locally nilpotent. The corresponding <math>\mathbb{G}_a</math>-actions are translations: <math>t\cdot x_{i}=x_{i}+t</math>, <math>t\cdot x_{j}=x_{j}</math> for <math>j\neq i</math>.

=== Example 2 (Freudenburg's (2,5)-homogeneous derivation) ===
Source:<ref name="Fr_(2,5)">{{cite journal|last1=Freudenburg|first1=G.|title=Actions of <math>\mathbb{G}_a</math> on <math>\mathbb{A}^{3}</math> defined by homogeneous derivations|journal=Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra|date=1998|volume=126|issue=1|pages=169–181|doi=10.1016/S0022-4049(96)00143-0|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Let <math>f_1=x_1x_3-x_2^2</math>, <math>f_2=x_3f_1^2+2x_1^2x_2f_1+x^5</math>, and let <math>\partial</math> be the Jacobian derivation <math display="inline">\partial(f_{3})=\det \left[\tfrac{\partial f_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}\right]_{i,j=1,2,3}</math>. Then <math>\partial\in \operatorname{LND}(k[x_1,x_2,x_3])</math> and <math>\operatorname{rank}\partial=3</math> (see [[#Triangular derivations|below]]); that is, <math>\partial</math> annihilates no variable. The fixed point set of the corresponding <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math>-action equals <math>\{x_1=x_2=0\}</math>.

=== Example 3 ===
Consider <math>Sl_2(k)=\{ad-bc=1\}\subseteq k^{4}</math>. The locally nilpotent derivation <math>a\tfrac{\partial}{\partial b}+c\tfrac{\partial}{\partial d}</math> of its coordinate ring corresponds to a natural action of <math>\mathbb{G}_a</math> on <math>Sl_2(k)</math> via right multiplication of upper triangular matrices. This action gives a nontrivial <math>\mathbb{G}_a</math>-bundle over <math>\mathbb{A}^{2}\setminus \{(0,0)\}</math>. However, if <math>k=\mathbb{C}</math> then this bundle is trivial in the smooth category<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Dubouloz|first1=A.|last2=Finston|first2=D.|title=On exotic affine 3-spheres|journal=J. Algebraic Geom.|date=2014|volume=23| issue=3|pages=445–469| doi=10.1090/S1056-3911-2014-00612-3| arxiv=1106.2900|s2cid=119651964 }}</ref>

== LND's of the polynomial algebra ==
Let <math>k</math> be a field of characteristic zero (using Kambayashi's theorem one can reduce most results to the case <math>k=\mathbb{C}</math><ref name="DK">{{cite journal|last1=Daigle|first1=D.|last2=Kaliman|first2=S.|title=A note on locally nilpotent derivations and variables of <math>k[X,Y,Z]</math>|journal=[[Canad. Math. Bull.]]|date=2009|volume=52|issue=4| pages=535–543|doi=10.4153/CMB-2009-054-5|doi-access=free|url=http://www.math.miami.edu/~kaliman/library/canada.daigle-kaliman.pdf}}</ref>) and let <math>A=k[x_1,\dots, x_n]</math> be a polynomial algebra.

=== {{math|1=''n'' = 2}} ({{math|'''G'''<sub>''a''</sub>}}-actions on an affine plane)===
{{math theorem | name = Rentschler's theorem | math_statement =
Every LND of <math>k[x_1,x_2]</math> can be conjugated to <math>f(x_1)\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x_2}</math> for some <math>f(x_1)\in k[x_1]</math>. This result is closely related to the fact that every [[automorphism]] of an [[affine plane]] is [[Tame abstract elementary class|tame]], and does not hold in higher dimensions.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Rentschler|first1=R.|title=Opérations du groupe additif sur le plan affine|journal=Comptes Rendus de l'Académie des Sciences, Série A-B|date=1968|volume=267|pages=A384–A387}}</ref>}}

=== {{math|1=''n'' = 3}} ({{math|'''G'''<sub>''a''</sub>}}-actions on an affine 3-space)===
{{math theorem | name = [[Masayoshi Miyanishi|Miyanishi]]'s theorem | math_statement =
The kernel of every nontrivial LND of <math>A=k[x_1,x_2,x_3]</math> is isomorphic to a polynomial ring in two variables; that is, a fixed point set of every nontrivial <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math>-action on <math>\mathbb{A}^{3}</math> is isomorphic to <math>\mathbb{A}^{2}</math>.<ref>{{cite book|last1=Miyanishi|first1=M.|contribution=Normal affine subalgebras of a polynomial ring|title=Algebraic and Topological Theories (Kinosaki, 1984)|date=1986|pages=37–51|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/41754985}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|last1=Sugie|first1=T.|chapter=Algebraic Characterization of the Affine Plane and the Affine 3-Space |title=Topological Methods in Algebraic Transformation Groups (New Brunswick, NJ, 1988)|volume=80|date=1989| pages=177–190|doi=10.1007/978-1-4612-3702-0_12|isbn=978-1-4612-8219-8|publisher=Birkhäuser Boston|series=Progress in Mathematics}}</ref>

In other words, for every <math>0\neq \partial \in \operatorname{LND}(A)</math> there exist <math>f_{1},f_{2}\in A</math> such that <math>\ker\partial=k[f_{1},f_{2}]</math> (but, in contrast to the case <math>n=2</math>, <math>A</math> is not necessarily a polynomial ring over <math>\ker \partial</math>). In this case, <math>\partial</math> is a Jacobian derivation: <math display="inline">\partial(f_{3}) = \det\left[\tfrac{\partial f_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}\right]_{i,j=1,2,3}</math>.<ref name="Daigle">{{cite journal|last1=D.|first1=Daigle|title=On kernels of homogeneous locally nilpotent derivations of <math>k[X,Y,Z]</math>|journal=Osaka J. Math.|date=2000|volume=37|issue=3|pages=689–699|url=https://projecteuclid.org/download/pdf_1/euclid.ojm/1200789363}}</ref>}}

{{math theorem | name = Zurkowski's theorem | math_statement =
Assume that <math>n=3</math> and <math>\partial\in \operatorname{LND}(A)</math> is homogeneous relative to some positive grading of <math>A</math> such that <math>x_1,x_2,x_3</math> are homogeneous. Then <math>\ker\partial=k[f,g]</math> for some homogeneous <math>f,g</math>. Moreover,<ref name="Daigle" /> if <math>\deg x_{1},\deg x_{2},\deg x_{3}</math> are relatively prime, then <math>\deg f,\deg g</math> are relatively prime as well.<ref>{{cite web|last1=Zurkowski|first1=V.D.|title=Locally finite derivations|url=http://www.math.ru.nl/~maubach/Research/zurkowski.pdf}}</ref><ref name="Freudenburg" />}}

{{math theorem | name = Bonnet's theorem | math_statement =
A quotient morphism <math>\mathbb{A}^{3}\to \mathbb{A}^{2}</math> of a <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math>-action is [[Surjective function|surjective]]. In other words, for every <math>0\neq \partial \in \operatorname{LND}(A)</math>, the embedding <math>\ker\partial\subseteq A</math> induces a surjective morphism <math>\operatorname{Spec}A\to \operatorname{Spec}\ker\partial</math>.<ref name="Bonnet">{{cite journal|last1=Bonnet|first1=P.|title=Surjectivity of quotient maps for algebraic <math>(\mathbb{C},+)</math>-actions and polynomial maps with contractible fibers|journal=Transform. Groups|date=2002|volume=7|issue=1|pages=3–14|doi=10.1007/s00031-002-0001-6|arxiv=math/0602227}}</ref><ref name="Kaliman" />

This is no longer true for <math>n\geqslant 4</math>, e.g. the image of a quotient map <math>\mathbb{A}^{4}\to\mathbb{A}^{3}</math> by a <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math>-action <math>t\cdot (x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)=(x_1,x_2,x_3-tx_2,x_4+tx_1)</math> (which corresponds to a LND given by <math>x_1\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x_4}-x_2\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x_3})</math> equals <math>\mathbb{A}^{3}\setminus \{(x_1,x_2,x_3): x_{1}=x_{2}=0,x_{3}\neq 0\}</math>.}}

{{math theorem | name = [[Shulim Kaliman|Kaliman]]'s theorem | math_statement =
Every fixed-point free action of <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math> on <math>\mathbb{A}^{3}</math> is conjugate to a translation. In other words, every <math>\partial \in \operatorname{LND}(A)</math> such that the image of <math>\partial</math> generates the unit ideal (or, equivalently, <math>\partial</math> defines a nowhere vanishing vector field), admits a slice. This results answers one of the conjectures from [[Challenging problems on affine n-space|Kraft's list]].<ref name="Kaliman">{{cite journal|last1=Kaliman|first1=S.|title=Free <math>\mathbb{C}_{+}</math>-actions on <math>\mathbb{C}^3</math> are translations|journal=Invent. Math.|date=2004|volume=156|issue=1|pages=163–173|doi=10.1007/s00222-003-0336-1|url=http://www.math.miami.edu/~kaliman/library/Ka.invent.2004.c+.pdf|arxiv=math/0207156|s2cid=15769378 }}</ref>

Again, this result is not true for <math>n\geqslant 4</math>:<ref name="Winkelmann">{{cite journal|last1=Winkelmann|first1=J.|title=On free holomorphic <math>\mathbb{C}</math>-actions on <math>\mathbb{C}^n</math> and homogeneous Stein manifolds|journal=[[Math. Ann.]]|date=1990|volume=286|issue=1–3|pages=593–612|doi=10.1007/BF01453590|doi-access=free|url=http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/pdfcache/PPN235181684_0286/PPN235181684_0286___LOG_0038.pdf}}</ref> e.g. consider the <math>x_1\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x_2}+ x_2\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x_3}+(x_2^2-2x_1 x_3-1)\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{4}}\in \operatorname{LND}(\mathbb{C}[x_{1},x_{2},x_{3},x_{4}])</math>. The points <math>(x_1,1,0,0)</math> and <math>(x_1,-1,0,0)</math> are in the same orbit of the corresponding <math>\mathbb{G}_a</math>-action if and only if <math>x_{1}\neq 0</math>; hence the (topological) quotient is not even Hausdorff, let alone homeomorphic to <math>\mathbb{C}^{3}</math>.}}

{{math theorem | name = Principal ideal theorem | math_statement =
Let <math>\partial\in\operatorname{LND}(A)</math>. Then <math>A</math> is [[flat morphism|faithfully flat]] over <math>\ker\partial</math>. Moreover, the ideal <math>\ker \partial \cap \operatorname{im}\partial</math> is [[Principal ideal|principal]] in <math>A</math>.<ref name="DK" />}}

=== Triangular derivations ===
Let <math>f_1,\dots,f_n</math> be any system of variables of <math>A</math>; that is, <math>A=k[f_1,\dots, f_n]</math>. A derivation of <math>A</math> is called ''[[triangular derivation|triangular]]'' with respect to this system of variables, if <math>\partial f_1\in k</math> and <math>\partial f_{i} \in k[f_1,\dots,f_{i-1}]</math> for <math>i=2,\dots,n</math>. A derivation is called ''triangulable'' if it is conjugate to a triangular one, or, equivalently, if it is triangular with respect to some system of variables. Every triangular derivation is locally nilpotent. The converse is true for <math>\leq 2</math> by Rentschler's theorem above, but it is not true for <math>n\geq 3</math>.

;Bass's example
The derivation of <math>k[x_1,x_2,x_3]</math> given by <math>x_1\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x_2}+2x_2x_1\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x_3}</math> is not triangulable.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Bass|first1=H.|title=A non-triangular action of <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math> on <math>\mathbb{A}^{3}</math>|journal=Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra|date=1984|volume=33|issue=1|pages=1–5|doi=10.1016/0022-4049(84)90019-7|doi-access=free}}</ref> Indeed, the fixed-point set of the corresponding <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math>-action is a quadric cone <math>x_2x_3=x_2^2</math>, while by the result of Popov,<ref>{{cite book|last1=Popov|first1=V. L.|title=Algebraic Groups Utrecht 1986 |chapter=On actions of <math>\mathbb{G}_a</math> on <math>\mathbb{A}^n</math> |volume=1271|pages=237–242|doi=10.1007/BFb0079241|series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics|year=1987|isbn=978-3-540-18234-4}}</ref> a fixed point set of a triangulable <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math>-action is isomorphic to <math>Z\times \mathbb{A}^{1}</math> for some affine variety <math>Z</math>; and thus cannot have an isolated singularity.

{{math theorem | name = Freudenburg's theorem | math_statement =
The above necessary geometrical condition was later generalized by Freudenburg.<ref name="Freudenburg_tr">{{cite journal|last1=Freudenburg|first1=G.|title=Triangulability criteria for additive group actions on affine space|journal=J. Pure Appl. Algebra|date=1995|volume=105|issue=3|pages=267–275|doi=10.1016/0022-4049(96)87756-5|doi-access=free}}</ref> To state his result, we need the following definition:

A [[corank]] of <math>\partial\in \operatorname{LND}(A)</math> is a maximal number <math>j</math> such that there exists a system of variables <math>f_1,\dots, f_n</math> such that <math>f_1,\dots, f_j\in\ker\partial</math>. Define <math>\operatorname{rank}\partial</math> as <math>n</math> minus the corank of <math>\partial</math>.

We have <math>1\leq \operatorname{rank}\partial \leq n</math> and <math>\operatorname{rank}(\partial)=1</math> if and only if in some coordinates, <math>\partial=h\tfrac{\partial}{\partial x_{n}}</math> for some <math>h\in k[x_1,\dots,x_{n-1}]</math>.<ref name="Freudenburg_tr" />

Theorem: If <math>\partial\in \operatorname{LND}(A)</math> is triangulable, then any hypersurface contained in the fixed-point set of the corresponding <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math>-action is isomorphic to <math>Z\times \mathbb{A}^{\operatorname{rank} \partial}</math>.<ref name="Freudenburg_tr" />

In particular, LND's of maximal rank <math>n</math> cannot be triangulable. Such derivations do exist for <math>n\geq 3</math>: the first example is the ''(2,5)-homogeneous derivation'' (see above), and it can be easily generalized to any <math>n\geq 3</math>.<ref name="Fr_(2,5)" />}}

== Makar-Limanov invariant ==
{{Main|Makar-Limanov invariant}}

The intersection of the kernels of all locally nilpotent derivations of the coordinate ring, or, equivalently, the ring of invariants of all <math>\mathbb{G}_{a}</math>-actions, is called "Makar-Limanov invariant" and is an important algebraic invariant of an affine variety. For example, it is trivial for an affine space; but for the [[Koras–Russell cubic threefold]], which is [[Diffeomorphism|diffeomorphic]] to <math>\mathbb{C}^{3}</math>, it is not.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Kaliman|first1=S.|last2=Makar-Limanov|first2=L.|title=On the Russell-Koras contractible threefolds|journal=J. Algebraic Geom.|date=1997|volume=6|issue=2|pages=247–268}}</ref>
